Yes. we have adopted a new name. 

For nearly 20 years you have known 
us as Galloway Publishing Co., and 
as publishers of CAMPING MAG¬ 
AZINE, official publication of Ameri¬ 
can Camping Association. 

Now wc have broadened our services 
to camping, and changed our name to 
Galloway Corporation, so that it more 
accurately represents the new breadth 
in our activities. 

In 1965, in addition to continuing 
publication of CAMPING 
MAGAZINE, our organization 
will further serve by managing the 
commercial exhibits of ACA Regional 
Conventions in Kansas City, Mo., 
Columbus, Ohio, and Syracuse, N.Y. 
In 1966, we will manage the exhibits 
for ACA’s National Convention in 
Chicago. 

Still further services to camping— 
and to YOU—are in the planning 
stage. We will announce them as they 
become operational. 

GALLOWAY CORPORATION 

- Serving Camping Since 1946 -

"ACCREDITATION" 

BOON OB BUGABOO 


by W. E. Yard , 
General Secretary , 
Sault Ste. Marie Y.M.C.A. 


An old friend recently purchased a 
new house. Several weeks after moving 
in, an inspector called to check the 
wiring. Days later, another electrical 
inspector came along, and then one 
day the householder received a framed 
certificate and a “gold” sticker . . . 
hers was a “gold medallion home”! 
Perhaps this unique recognition was 
important to her, but when she affixed 
to sticker to an obscure fuse box in the 
basement, and used the certificate 
frame for a charming picture of her 
young son and his dog . . . we won¬ 
dered—how valid were these particular 
criteria in recognizing a good “home”? 

For many years camping people in 
the United States and Canada have 
wrestled with the problems of “raising 
standards”. Much progress has been 
made, but how much more might have 
been achieved had we avoided confus- 
sing “Accreditation” with “Raising of 
Standards”. At times the zealous advo¬ 
cates of “recognition symbols” have 
waged an all-out struggle for the 
acceptance of the “inspection, accredi¬ 
tation, recognition” pattern for camp¬ 
ing association work in this field. 

Let us get ourselves into perspective! 
No one (as yet) has to belong to the 
camping association. It is still a volun¬ 
tary association of people and organ¬ 
izations who come together ostensibly 
for the improvement of camping prac¬ 
tices. Docs the growing pressure for 
this voluntary body to become a legis¬ 
lative organization reflect the tendency 


of one segment of the membership to 
refute the original concept in favour 
of a sort of modern-day “craft guild”? 
Some members have likened the devel¬ 
opment they see ahead for the camp¬ 
ing association to the development of 
an organization such as the medical 
association. To this writer the analogy 
does not seem a good one, particularly 
in view of the original purposes of our 
association and its unusually hetero¬ 
geneous constituency. 

The visit of one camp director to 
another, preceded by a “self-evalua¬ 
tion” at the visited camp is a sound 
educational procedure. Some years ago 
the Ontario Cantping Association re¬ 
quired that, as a demonstration of 
their espousement of the association 
purposes, new members must agree to 
participate in a programme of “self- 
evaluation”. This seems commendable 
and constructive, but does it provide a 
basis for giving special recognition to 
any camp or group of camps? The 
visit itself may involve a four-or five- 
hour attempt to learn something about 
a camp which is spread over hundreds 
of acres, involves hundreds of campers 
and employs dozens of staff. The gar¬ 
bage pit may be well‘Covered, the 
windows may be well screened, the 
medical arrangements may be satis¬ 
factory, but how can a visitor assess the 
really vital factors of “leadership moti¬ 
vation” and “character development 
potential” about which every parent is 
concerned ? 


48 


Canadian Camping 





“Hold on”, say the accreditation 
folks, “we don’t recommend anybody 
—we just put the names of certain 
camps in bold type in our directory, 
or list them in a special way” . . . isn’t 
this really splitting hairs? 

“They accredit camps in the States” 
is another frequent argument . . but 
surely, in this field above all others we 
in Canada do not have to follow some¬ 
one else’s lead. For our organization 
in our country we might have the cour¬ 
age to believe that voluntary, non- 
coercivc, educative procedures will 
achieve the greatest results. 

Our organized camping movement 
has sometimes been described as one 
of the few really new developments in 
the field of education in the last half 
century. Within the association itself 
the voluntary participation of inter¬ 
ested members is consistent with this 
educational approach . . . and yet some 
would embark upon a programme 
which, is not unlike giving a “general 
proficiency award 55 to those whose 
penmanship is good. We aren’t equip¬ 
ped to test in other fields but somehow 
vve rationalize that this award is so im¬ 
portant to some that it must be granted 
and then we must take all possible steps 
to try to assure the public that by giv¬ 
ing this recognition we do not really 
intend to convey the impression of 
overall commendation which we rec¬ 
ognize they will assume. 

Accreditation and recognition, no 
matter how subtle, will tend to discour¬ 
age many who feel they are being 
carried along quite a different stream 
from that down which they first began 
to paddle when they joined a camping 
association. Rather than that volun¬ 
tary association of people and organ¬ 
izations, they find themselves in one 
list or another—in bold type or plain. 
One is reminded of Edwin Markham’s 
short poem, 

“He drew a circle and left me out 

Heretic, rebel, a thing to flout 


But love and I had the wit to win 
We drew a circle and took him in”. 

Surely our function has traditionally 
been that of drawing circles to bring 
people in, and then, through positive 
educative procedures, to help them 
achieve a higher standard of camping 
practices. 

Let us recognize that the symbols of 
recognition and approval have been 
and always will be very important to 
some individuals in the camping field. 
One doubts however whether it is 
appropriate to reshape an association 
to met the needs of a small segment. 
If we are being pushed in the direction 
of becoming a legislative organization 
—and there are those who feel we are 
—we must recognize the fact that the 
legislative and educative functions may 
not be mutually supportive—nor even 
complimentary when assigned to a 
single organization. 

Regardless of how many forms we 
may fill out or how often we may plod 
around a camp-site looking at physical 
facilities, the most important criteria 
of any camp is the philosophy and 
motivation of the person who directs 
it. The function of a camping associa¬ 
tion may well be to deepen the under¬ 
standings, improve the skills and en¬ 
rich the philosophy of camp directors. 

Perhaps one day camp directors will 
be “accredited”. If and when they are, 
some “professional society of directors” 
should play an important role. The 
emergence of such a society as a result 
of study and discussions within the 
membership of the Camping Associa¬ 
tion seems a distinctly possible and 
wholly appropriate development . . . 
but once it develops let us not confuse 
it with the Camping Association . . . 
Let it be a separate entity! The old 
concept of voluntary participation is 
one to be guarded jealously — our 
function is not to draw circles that 
leave people out! 

- • 


Toronto, Canada, February 1965 


49 



OUR 

CABANA 

by Louise Casselman 


An International 
Experience 
in Mexico 


On the southern slope of a lush 
green hill in the Sierra Madres, forty- 
seven miles from Mexico City, lies 
“Our Cabana”, an international centre 
owned and operated by the World 
Association of Girl Guides and Girl 
Scouts. Only two miles from the heart 
of Cuernavaca in the State of Morelos, 
this residential abode, whose wide-open 
doors welcome all members of the 
movement, was built and is now main¬ 
tained through the generosity of con¬ 
tributions from every part of the globe. 
Since 1957, girls from many lands have 
gathered at Our Cabana to strengthen 
the friendship bonds between all 
nations and all races. These gather¬ 
ings have been named after Juliette 
Low, in memory of her work and de¬ 
votion to Scouting in the United States 
as well as on the International level. 

Last summer, forty of us from 
Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, 
Chile, Colombia, Ghana, India, Mex¬ 
ico, Netherlands, Norway, Peru, South 
Africa and the U.S.A., arrived in 
Mexico with open minds and hearts 
only to learn how narrow the mind can 
really be, and how unfeeling the heart. 

Spirit and mind were aroused during 
our brief encounter in the Sierra Mad¬ 
res. Unusual crafts and strange food 
opened our eyes to some of the talents 
and ways of our friends in other lands. 
As two South Americans debated their 


interests and concerns at the breakfast 
table, Belgian ears cocked to catch the 
swift Spanish phrases. Soon we learned 
to respond to the rhythm of a South 
African chant and just as eagerly to 
dance the dynamic Mexican “Bomba”. 
Group discussion ranging from gover- 
ment policies to marriage customs ac¬ 
cented our differences as surely as they 
underlined a certain similarity of feel¬ 
ing and a bond of faith. 

Only when we learn to accept these 
differences for their true worth, only 
when we realize that one nation can¬ 
not impose its whole philosophy on 
another, can we contribute significantly 
to international understanding, and to 
peaceful co-existence in its full and true 
meaning of the expression. 

The adventure we shared is one 
which must be shared by all. Having 
taken to Our Cabana only ourselves 
and a keeness to learn, we returned 
with some knowledge of five races, ten 
creeds, thirteen nations and, most im¬ 
portant of all, thirty-nine new friend¬ 
ships. We also returned with a new 
understanding. Living is but an end¬ 
less process of the opening of the heart 
and broadening of the mind. In the 
experiences at Our Cabana are cradled 
the beginning of this continuous pursuit 
of knowledge and wisdom. Is there a 
better way to achieve international 
peace? 


50 


Canadian Camping 



SECOND THOUGHTS 

OF A PARENT 


One of the features of the 1964 Ontario Camping Association 
Conference was a panel discussion by parents of campers. Men¬ 
tioned at the time, when all was said and done, was the fact that 
this particular group of parents presented a rosy picture of the 
whole field of organized camping, with little or no criticism, con¬ 
structive or otherwise. Mr. Lloyd Minshall, who was one of the 
panel participants, mulled over the whole question, with the result 
that he has given us further food for thought in the work that 
concerns all of 11 s. 


Perhaps things sounded all too 
patsy-patsy on the panel—especially 
when we ended on the note we did. 
Perhaps parents are not the right 
people to give constructive criticism. 
Perhaps we do not think at all about 
the kind of questions we were asked. 

How about your camp sites? The 
fight for land use in Ontario just start¬ 
ing. How many actually hold the deed 
to a buffer strip around the area now 
used? How many own that favourite 
spot for outtrips? Maybe next year 
it will be privately owned, and by 
someone who is not very tolerant of 
noisy campers. 

How many use good conservation 
practices? Is there an area on your 
sites that would be better reforested; 
and has any effort been made to carry 
it out? Conservation, the compliment 
to nature lore, should be taught by 
someone trained in the subject. There 
are now enough Conservation Authori¬ 
ties and Fieldmcn to make this possible. 
Conservation, as such, did not seem to 
be featured at your conference. 


Toronto , Canada , February 1965 


Do you use pictures to the best 
advantage? Many campers bring 
cameras and take home a roll of ex¬ 
posed film. But do enough counsellors 
see that some of these pictures accur¬ 
ately represent the program? No camp 
needs a photographer on staff' but, per¬ 
haps, a few picture projects will tell 
the story to the parent, and even 
supplement the one-paragraph letter 
sent home on the weekend. 

Is anyone encouraging the trend to¬ 
ward family camping? Facilities and 
opportunities for this programme are 
still needed. And this does not mean 
packing a lunch for Father and send¬ 
ing him off fishing while Mother keeps 
fit in the recreation hall and Junior is 
herded off on a hike. Perhaps there 
is now sufficient interest to enter this 
field commercially. Is it worth finding 
out? 

Has anyone tried an international 
camp? We are very conscious of this 
today and try to bring people face to 
face in many different settings. Is it 
being done in camping? 


51 




Summer classes in secondary schools 
for students who need to brush up in 
one or two subjects are now successful. 
Could this idea be moved to a camp 
setting? 

Students from across Canada have 
been brought together to form an or¬ 
chestra. Could all cultural activities 
be encouraged in the same way in sum¬ 
mer camps? Does anyone care enough 
to try? 

Even with the upsurge in day camp¬ 
ing, is enough effort being made to 
bring the camping experience within 
reach of all who would like it? Is it 
fair to assume welfare agencies and ser¬ 
vice clubs should carry this out? Could 
private camps help meet the need for 
at least one week each summer? 

In spite of what is said, there is a 
tendency to lean towards the glossy, 
the posh and the sophisticated. Should 
not the camp experience be kept as 
simple and as close to nature as 
possible ? 

In fact, has the O.C.A. ever con¬ 
sidered setting up a brainstorming 
session to explore the future of camp¬ 
ing? This could not be done in a 



general session at the anual conference 
as only general platitudes would come. 
Let those who brainstorm represent a 
cross section of the association, but 
make sure they are uninhibited in their 
thinking. Even if only three or four 
gems emerge from the ideas, it will 
have been worthwhile. 

Regardless of what the panel said, 
there is, and always will be, room for 
improvement in leadership. While the 
majority of private owners and agen¬ 
cies try hard to find and train that 
mythical “perfect” counsellor, it is sus¬ 
pected there are quite a number who 
do not even come close. It is known 
that many short-term camps are 
staffed with leadership that is found 
too casually, too late to be adequately 
trained and too poorly rewarded to 
really care. 

Yes, even in the area of leadership 
there is no room for complacency. No, 
this is not the time to relax and just 
“scratch each others back.” 


Editorial Policy 

re “Accreditation" 

Your Editorial Committee has asked 
the Executive of our Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association what they would like 
our policy to be in considering for 
publication subjects of a controversial 
nature. At a recent meeting their 
Executive passed the following motion: 

“That the Editorial Committee of 
CANADIAN CAMPING be encour¬ 
aged to accept controversial material 
for publication. If necessary, a clause 
may be included indicating that the 
views of the author do not necessarily 
reflect the views of the C.C.A.” 


52 


Canadian Camping 


We’ll warn you right from the start: 
once smitten by the urge to collect, 
identify and study rocks, fossils and 
minerals, all hope vanishes for ever 
again hiking in an upright position. 
Suddenly, every stone underfoot be¬ 
comes a probable rarity, every sparkle 
a potential diamond, and every yellow 
pyrite-like streak possible gold. It’s all 
in the mind, of course; but these are 
the unmistakable marks, hopes and as¬ 
pirations of that freak of the human 
species, The Rock Hound. 

However, if you show these tenden¬ 
cies, take heart. You’re in line as a 
Guiding Light, that person so vitally 
necessary to -any geology programme. 
Without you, the activity can never 
get off the ground. 

With us it was a natural from the 
first; although, like so many insidious 
things in life, it was upon us before 
we knew it. Our gem of a George who 
hauls and hammers, paints and repairs 
all summer long, was fortunate (we’re 
convinced) in being a former mine 
worker during the Rush when every 
farmer’s field was fair game for 
Uranium, and every North Country 
lane the fanciful road to untold wealth. 

George started it all by showing us 
some of his urananite and zircon 
specimens. That was all we needed. 
We commandeered him to lead us on 
our first cross-countiy jaunts to former 
mines and trenchings for fluorite and 
apatite. We were fired with zeal. Came 
more questions. Where could we find 
quartz? Beryl? Tourmaline? We 
found them. We brought them back to 
camp, and the whole programme was 
launched for better, for worse, and 
most certainly for richer in experience 
and knowledge. 

Enthusiasm takes care of itself in 
this type of programme. Reference

SO 

YOU 

HAVE 

ROCKS 

IN 

THE 

HEAD? 


Then get busy 
and ciystalize a natural 
programme your 
campers can 
enjoy, wherever you 
are, in any part of 
Canada ... for 
the rocks are always 
with us. 


by Eanswylhe Flynn, 

Camp Brigadoon for Girls 


Toronto , Canada , February 1965 


53 



books are now on every bookstand, and 
easy to read. Cnee the Guiding Light 
can produce samples of the most com¬ 
mon pegmatites, schists, quartz, micas 
or feldspars, can put the proper names 
to them and tell something of their 
weight, hardness, quality and use, the 
programme is on . . . always, at camp, 



at the amateur level. We suggest that 
it does not become a deep scientific 
project except for the few who wish a 
little advanced study. It is more fun 
for everyone if it remains a new and 
open field for all, an absorbing interest 
and most certainly not compulsory for 
every camper. 

It isn’t long before everybody is on 
the bandwagon; but introduce the sub¬ 
ject casually and slowly, if not slyly. 
The first hikes and discovery trips can 
be just that . . . explorations for rocks 
if any campers want to look for them, 
with games for those who don’t and 
a picnic supper for all. Don’t prolong 
it. Keep it short so that the group will 
demand a repeat performance soon. 
Any rock samples should be brought 
back to camp and immediately com¬ 
pared with pictures and information 
in reference books so that names can 
be given the Finds. 

Casually, on the next day, perhaps, 
the counsellor-in-charge might sit out¬ 
side the Craft Shop or any other 
central spot, chopping the rocks into 
smaller pieces, selecting them, categor¬ 
izing them for display purposes. At 
this point, interest on the part of 


campers begins to deepen and without 
efFort. Passers-by stop to look. Those 
who might not be interested in other 
activities may suddenly want to know 
more about rocks and their formation. 
The interest spreads and deepens, and 
before long, samples are gathered on 
the camp site, on other hikes and 
canoe trips. Names arc learned, colours 
and crystal formations identified. In 
less than no time, campers will suggest 
the founding of a Mineral or Geology 
club, and soon afterwards ask for a 
special place, tent or corner of a build¬ 
ing for display purposes. In our case, 
the idea took on so thoroughly that we 
built a special cabin, 9' x 12' in size 
with two rows of divided shelving to 
hold our forty-or-more samples, each 
bearing a card which names the sample 
in the section. Our stone tumbler sits 
on one corner table for the polishing 
of future pendants, cuff links, earrings 
and key chain stones. Books, tools and 
other equipment appear on the op¬ 
posite table, the whole room a very 
busy place indeed, and an attraction 
for other cam]) groups when they visit 
us at any time during the summer. 

Best part of the whole programme is 
that it requires only a small financial 
outlay to set it up. Samples, equipment 
and reference books can be kept in a 
special tent or a corner of the Rec¬ 
reation Flail or Lodge. 

HAVERSACKS, fruit baskets, 
bushel hampers should be in fair supply 
for each trip, since too many samples 
cannot be carried at one time in one 
container, especially by young campers. 
Take ten to twelve containers on each 
trip so that no one will be overloaded 
on the return journey. 

ROCK CHISELS. HAND PICKS 
and a STONE HAMMER make the 
gathering of samples possible; and the 
leader must first give a short course in 
the safe handling of such tools to avoid 
the possibility of smashed fingers or 


54 


Canadian Camping 


toes. Stress should also be placed on 
care of tools, for they can be easily 
forgotten and lost in the excitement 
of a Find. 

The eyes should be covered when 
rocks are being hammered or chipped, 
and by this we mean by some sort of 
glasses or goggles. Rock splinters are 



sharp as glass and can get into the 
eye and cause untold damage. One 
can purchase goggles for rock hunters, 
but we have used ski gogles and under¬ 
water goggles most successfully. 

BOOKS. The market is rife with 
books which serve to acquaint amateur, 
student or seasoned Rock Hound with 
minerals, rocks and fossils, known and 
rare. 

THE FIELD GUIDE TO ROCKS 
AND MINERALS by Pough is the 
standard general reference book, as 
lavishly illustrated and as full of infor¬ 
mation as the Field Guide to Birds. 

GETTING ACQUAINTED WITH 
ROCKS AND MINERALS by Eng¬ 
lish and Jensen, presents to the student 
a well organized list of rocks names, 
pictures and descriptive information in 
alphabetical order. The advantage of 
this book is the addition of two or 
three chapters on equipment, how to 
look for rocks, where to find them 
and how to display them. 

Search the bookstores. Pocket books, 
“Trend” books, paper-back, cloth-bound 
editions on gems, stone-cutting, jewel¬ 
lery making, they are with us for the 
searching, any size, any price. 


Do be sure of thorough supervision 
on field trips, for there is great danger 
in campers wandering off on their own, 
thinking only of the excitement of ex¬ 
ploration and discovery. Field trips 
should be taken only in small groups, 
in the company of only alert and com¬ 
petent counsellors. Any abandoned 
mining or trenching area is bound to 
be strewn with caves varying in size 
from mammoth, cathedral-like cut¬ 
tings, to the small but tempting under¬ 
ground variety. Keep campers away 
from the inside of the small caves. 
Usually they are shored up. This, in 
itself, gives warning. They can collapse. 
Noise vibration, chipping, hammering, 
tramping feet overhead can tumble 
tons of rock on to unsuspecting bodies. 
Edges of any earth cavities or craters 
can give way when they have been 
open to the elements for a long time. 
Many craters are filled with water, 
and are bottomless. 

Any ancient shafts or adits must be 
avoided. The wood has rotted away; 
rusty spikes and nails protrude where 
they are least expected. Water runs in 
from springs. Further, rock samples 
are never found around mine entrances 
or shafts. Trenchings are the best 
source of supply. 

There should be as much alert super¬ 
vision on field trips as there is on the 
waterfront, for the same enthusiasm 
prevails, and one slip could lose a life. 

We would venture to say that there 
isn’t a camp across the continent that 
could not use this type of programme 
in some form. Each province can boast 
its own fossil, rock and mineral forma¬ 
tion. each differing from the other. 
Study your own particular area. Pro¬ 
vincial Departments of Mines will 
assist. Make use of it. Get the campers 
interested. Play it for all it is worth, 
but Play It Safe. 


Toronto , Canada , February 1965

tttt 


®nber tfje g>tin 

by Elizabeth Raymer, 

Camp Tanamakoon 


Look at your hand. Examine it 
carefully. You are looking at one of 
the most advanced and complicated 
mechanisms in this world—nerve fibre, 
blood vessels, tendon ligament, bone, 
cartilage, skin, nails, tissue all so linked 
by muscles that the hand can perform 
everything from very strong, as taking 
the top off a jar, to the delicate action 
of threading a needle. It is a tool that 
no scientist has yet been able to dupli¬ 
cate. Yet each of us has been given 
two of these marvellous tools. As one 
verse goes:— 

No man can feel himself alone 
The while he bravely stands 
Between the best friends ever known 
His two, good, honest hands. 

—(Waterman) 

Hands have inspired painters and 
photographers to spend ages trying to 
capture the character and beauty they 
express. We look at hands and say 
that is an artistic hand or a practical 
hand, a hand with a stubborn thumb. 
The sight of a little baby’s hands moves 
our hearts to tenderness. Swinbourne 
called them “the sweetest flowers in 
all the world”. There are symphony 
conductors who will be remembered 
always for the magic their hands pro¬ 
duced in drawing music from their 
orchestras. Sculptors have used their 
hands to produce masterpieces which 
will live forever. Actors and actresses 
speak to vast audiences with eloquent 


hands. There have been love songs 
written about hands. I recommend 
that if you are ever perplexed over the 
choice of a topic for an essay next 
winter that you explore the subject of 
hands. The challenge to the imagina¬ 
tion is limitless; one can find quotations 
by the hundreds. One need only sit in 
a room and imagine what hands 
created all the things about one and 
never have to open a reference book, 
except perhaps the dictionary. 

Hands are symbols too. The open 
hand we recogni/c as generous and 
giving. The outstretched hand ex¬ 
presses the unspoken offer of communi¬ 
cation with another human being. 

“Art thou lonely, o my brother? 
Share thy little with another; 
Stretch a hand to one unfriended 
And thy loneliness is ended. 

—(Oxenham) 

The Golden Hand is a symbol all of 
you who have been Guides or Brownies 
know and respect. We have heard over 
and over of the hand that rocks the 
cradle is the hand that rules the world. 
Two right hands clasped and shaken 
may be the symbol of a firm agreement 
or fellowship. Two hands tenderly 
joined, the loving promise of the wed¬ 
ding ceremony. Upstrctched, out¬ 
stretched hands arc a benediction and 
a blessing. The armed fist denotes 
war and the strong hand clenched 
about a streak of lightning denotes 


56 


Canadian Camping 


power. Hands in the attitude of prayer 
create in the beholder a feeling of awe. 

But not all hands are good hands. 
There is the cunning hand of the thief; 
the malicious hand of the vandal; the 
tight-fisted hand of the selfish; the 
meddling, thoughtless hands, the envious 
hands, the greedy and snatching hand. 
My mother warned me frequently of 
the danger which lay in idle hands. 
She quoted the stern Isaac Watts— 
“For Satan finds some mischief still 
for idle hands to do”. 



We may laugh at that now, but its 
message is still valid. Idle hands often 
get into trouble, sometimes very griev¬ 
ous and serious trouble. 

As with all valuable tools you should 
take care of your hands, learn to use 
them properly, and not cut or break 
or damage them. You should keep 
them clean and train them well. Your 
hands tell much about your person¬ 
ality—they speak for you. Your hands 
may be clenched into fists to strike an¬ 
other, or they can be opened up to 
clasp his hand in friendship. Your 
hands can clutch the things you own as 
a miser does, or they can be opened as 
you give and share the things you 
possess. 

Your hands can fail helplessly by 
your side as a symbol of your sadness 
and failure, or they can be raised with 
joy to picture your faith and happiness. 
They can be trained to employ instru¬ 
ments of great usefulness or they can 
be used for destruction. How would a 
poet describe your hands? or the artist 


draw them? Are they good hands, are 
they idle hands, are they loving hands 
—or evil hands? 

If you go to art galleries or are fond 
of books on the subject of art, you have 
seen many paintings of Jesus as the 
particular artist imagined He must 
have looked. Always, His hands are 
most significant. They are dedicated 
hands gently laid on the head of a 
child or a suffering person. Those 
hands trained in the Carpenter’s skill 
knew usefulness. They were not idle 
hands. They were the hands of bless¬ 
ing, of healing, of inspiration. Oh! 
would that we could have such dedi¬ 
cated hands, hands which would be 
remembered only for their wonderful 
works! 

And when it came time for His 
suffering on the Cross to end, He cried 
“Father, into Thy hands I commend 
My spirit”. And with these words we 
arc reminded that our spirits too are 
in the hands of God. Those Almighty 
hands which have been through the 
ages the greatest of all sources of ins¬ 
piration, wonder and comfort. May 
the thought of those hands inspire each 
one of us now and forever more.

TRIBUTE AND WELCOME 
After six years of able leadership, 
Mr. Barry Lowes has given up the 
position as Chairman of the Editorial 
Committee. It is a position calling for 
patience, tact, haid-work and a broad 
interest in all things related to camping. 
All these things Mr. Lowes has in 
abundance and we are grateful to him 
for his tremendous contribution to the 
success of our magazine over the years. 
We are fortunate that he still feels able 
to serve on our Editorial Committee. 
In his pace as Chairman, we welcome 
Mr. Don Groff of the Kitchener 
YMCA, who has served his apprentice¬ 
ship under Mr. Lowes as a member of 
the committee for several years. 


Toronto , Canada , February 1965 


57 



TALES 

of a 


NATURE 

CABIN 


by 

Catherine Van Wagner 
Camp Notntnigue 


“It's the most interesting place in 
Camp”, said one ten-year-old camper, 
and his friend agreed with him as they 
browsed about the Nature Cabin. They 
asked “What’s new?” and checked the 
well-being of the three tiny fish caught 
in a strainer the day before. One was 
floating, tummy up, so they put in 
fresh water, another small plant and 
a sprinkle of fine fish food and went 
on their way, hoping to find the sur¬ 
vivors healthy next morning. 

Two small Monarch Caterpillars 
were found and added to the six al¬ 
ready munching fresh milkweed in a 
milk bottle placed in a screened cage. 
We arc “Assistant Researchers” in the 
Monarch Butterfly banding project 
carried on by the University of Tor¬ 
onto Zoology Department. Great was 
the interest in watching them eat and 
grow, and finally hang from a leaf or 
tlie roof of the cage to begin the meta¬ 
morphosis. We sometimes missed by 
minutes the shedding of the old faded 
skin and the amazing transformation to 
tlie beautiful green and gold dotted 
chrysalis. Equally fascinating is the 
sight of the brown and gold beauty 
feebly pulling itself out and clinging 
to the empty case to stretch and dry 
its wings. The day before the campers 
went home in August, there were five 
nearly full grown caterpillars feeding, 
but the morning after—an empty cage! 


Other pets were taken home, with the 
parents' permission. We hope that one 
mother had a scientific interest in 
caterpillars. 

Empty dragon fly nymph shells are 
picked from reeds and wharf posts, as 
well as adults not yet able to fly. These, 
with the live nymphs taken from the 
pond, complete another absorbing 
story of insect life. Similarly, the cic¬ 
ada shells on a tree illustrate the 
strange, almost unbelievcable seventeen 
vear cvcle of that noisy “hot weather 
bug”. ‘ 

A morning nature walk produces a 
varied “bag”: grasshoppers, crickets, a 
snake, a wolf spider carrying her egg 
sac; and seen arc carpenter ants at 
work in a stump; a vireo’s nest on a 
branch, low enough to be carefully 
pulled down to see the four tiny nest¬ 
lings with gaping yellow mouths; under 
a rotten log, centipedes, snails, adult 
and babies, strange mould forms, and 
the occasional salamander. Eggs were 
found one day with the baby sala¬ 
manders plainly seen squirming about 
in the shell. The hatching a few days 
later was a “Big Event” as was the 
birth of a family of garter snakes! All 
this, and becoming acquainted with 
trees and flowers, and the realization 
that we and all creatures arc depend¬ 
ent on green growing things for 
existence. 


58 


Canadian Camping 



Tadpoles of green leopard and bull 
frogs thrive in large jars of water with 
growing plants, and lettuce leaves to 
feed on. Here, collectors can go wild 
and have to be restrained—only three 
to a jar, please! 

load eggs arc easily found before 
camp season (just follow the trilling 
song in the shallows). They develop 
early in July into tiny bug sized toads. 
.Assorted sizes of Irogs, toads and 
snakes are found and identified. It is 
good for children to look on these 
small harmless creatures with interest. 
Too often the “kill it” instinct is upper¬ 
most. They learn their habits and how 
to keep them comfortable for a few 
days, then experience pleasure in see¬ 
ing them go free. An example of this 
is the following talc with a happy 
ending: 

One day four campers had caught a 
very small squirrel, probably on its 
first expedition with its mother, who 
was chattering furiously at the boys 
from a nearby tree. Baby was shiver¬ 
ing in a corner of the cage and its 
captors were admiring it. “What can 
we feed it?” Won’t it be fun to tame 
it!” “Could I take it home????” To 
all this there was only one answer. 
The group was silent a moment, then 
after some heated discussion “Let’s put 
it back in the tree”! The joyful reunion 
of mother and baby was a sight they 
will long remember with a good feeling. 

The Nature Cabin is a centre where 
the collecting urge is satisfied and 
steered into reasonable channels; where 
campers and counsellors can find out 
about things seen in the woods and 
fields, swamp, and water; a museum for 
permanent collections; a place for 
rainy day nature sessions, and the be¬ 
ginning and end of a Nature Trail. 
There is space for campers’ daily finds 
from which develop projects and ex¬ 
hibits—leaves, flowers, ferns, mosses, 
lichens, fungi, club mosses, horsetails, 
insects, edible plants and berries. From 
these, cabin visitors learn and are im¬ 


pressed by what others know and have 
accomplished. Hot Labrador Tea and 
cold sumac lemonade are served 
occasionally. All arc eager to taste and 
surprised comments follow, such as 
“Not bad!” Some even want “seconds”. 

Children love live pets—white mice 
and rabbits can be held, and are easily 
fed. Baby turtles arc fun at feeding 
time, staging a tug-of-war over a worm 
or snatching bits of hamburger from 
fingers. 

Add to all this activity a place for 
nature books for reference or to take 
out for Quiet Hour reading. “The most 
interesting place in camp?” For many 
children it can well be just that, and 
their enthusiasm is sure to spread. 
Many who were oblivious to nature 
begin to walk about with their eyes 
open to God’s wonderful world, and 
have their curiosity aroused as to what 
is going on there. 

All this interest is dependent in the 
first place on having a permanent staff 
member with a keen desire to intro¬ 
duce children to nature in the ideal 
camp surroundings, and make it an 
important part of the camp pro¬ 
gramme. Some knowledge of Nature 
Lore is very helpful, but enthusiasm is 
the keynote to which children respond 
—and teacher and campers will learn 
much together. 

Several years ago we were fortunate 
in having two senior staff members be¬ 
come interested in the Nature Pro¬ 
gramme. This gave a boost to the 
response of 14-15-year-old boys, most 
of whom seem to have a built-in 
prejudice about nature being for girls, 
or the very young. More seniors come 
now for morning instruction and some¬ 
times one hears “I didn’t know nature 
was so interesting”. This age, espec¬ 
ially, should be aware of the need for 
the wise use of all our natural re¬ 
sources, so Conservation is stressed in 
our nature programme, as well as on 
many other occasions in camp life.

FUNDAMENTALS OF FIRST AID 

A completely revised second edition 
of “The Fundamentals of First Aid” 
by Robert A. Mustard, M.B.E., B.A., 
M.D., F.R.C.S.(C), F.A.C.S., Assistant 
Professor, Department of Surgery, 
University of Toronto and Attending 
Surgeon, Toronto General Hospital, 
has now been issued by Porcupine Pub¬ 
lications Limited of Montreal by 
special arrangement with St. John's 
Ambulance, Canada, according to Nod 
J. Walsh, Vice-President of Porcupine 
Publications, a subsidiary of the Rolph- 
Clark-Stonc group of companies. 

Particular attention is drawn to the 
back cover of THE FUNDAMEN¬ 
TALS OF FIRST AID. A pcrusual of 
the “Preface” and the “Introductory 
Notes for Instructors” will outline the 
apparent revolutionary nature of the 
new text. Written for the layman, it 
avoids highly technical language, dis¬ 
cards some traditional practices which 



arc either unnecessary, ineffective or 
impractical, and introduces some new 
subjects such as oral resuscitation, ex¬ 
ternal heart massage, etc.

This new edition now becomes avail¬

price and will be of particular interest 
to families at sumer camp and to those

INSTANT FUN 

by Lorell Coffman Burns 

“You arc invited to enjoy fun un¬ 
limited via the pages of this original 
collection of quick-and-easy, time- 
tested fun-fare”, the jacket dedication 
says. “Add nothing to Instant Fun ex¬ 
cept the human ingredient . . . young, 
old, middling ... in quantities from 
two to two thousand. Mix, stir, 
sprinkle with laughter, and every time 
it turns out FUN!” A review of its 
chapters proves the truth of the state¬ 
ment. For the cabin counsellor who 
needs a supply of table quizzes or 
riddles for campers, for the programme 
director who must think up quick- 
quick games, skits and stunts, for the 
camp director who needs inspiration 
for light talk or an amusing address, 
the book is a boon and handy to carry 
around. G. R. Welch Company,

ALONG THE SEASHORE 

by Margaret Waring Buck 

An artist, a writer and a naturalist, 
Margaret Waring Buck has brought to 
young people the wonders of forest 


60 


Canadian Camping 


and field, pond and stream in an enter¬ 
taining and enlightening manner. 
Praised by naturalists, teachers and 
camp directors, her latest work opens 
up the world of simple marine life com¬ 
mon to young explorers and older 
amateurs. The writer begins with 
plants that grow beside the sea, and 
algae that grow in the sea, continuing 
on through sponges and corals, shell 
fish, ocean fish and birds of the seaside. 
Her chapters and illustrations on shell¬ 
fish and mollusks will be invaluable to 
those who collect shells as part of a 
camp programme or display. Each is 
illustrated and given its proper name 
so that there is no doubt about identi¬ 
fication. All of Miss Buck’s books are 
a decided asset to any camp library. 
G. R. Welch Company, Limited, Tor¬ 
onto 18. $3.25 in cloth; $1.95 in paper. 

RUNES OF THE NORTH 

by Sigurd F. Olson 

A rune in its general meaning, is a 
tale of magic and mystery. To Sigurd 
Olson this expresses his feelings about 
the haunting appeal of the wilderness 
and of the tales and legends to be 
found there. His runes are legends— 
yarns and wilderness reflections — 
drawn from the great northern vastness 
of Canada and Alaska. Whether he is 
recounting a charming Indian “myth” 
such as “The Dream Net” or describ¬ 
ing the exhilaration of the sauna, 
which is the primitive Finnish bath; or 
sharing the pleasures of digging a 
spring for a remote cabin in the woods, 
Olson evokes the eternal appeal of the 
wilds. 

RUNES OF THE NORTH is divi¬ 
ded into two sections: one, “Le Beau 
Pays”, reveals woodland lore of the land 
of big timber, rushing white water 
streams, and “lost” lakes of the Can¬ 
adian border; the other, “Pays d’en 
Haut”, has for the setting of its chap¬ 
ters the wilderness farther north, from 


Hudson’s Bay across the Barren 
Grounds and the tundra to the Yukon 
and Alaska. This latest book by the 
author of THE SINGING WILDER- 
NES, LISTENING POST, and THE 
LONELY LAND, will greatly please 
the thousands of readers who have 
found in him a kindred spirit—a man 
who puts into words their own deep 
feelings about nature. Robert Hine’s 
jacket drawing of the loon on a lovely 
lake, symbol of far-away places, and 
his atmospheric pen and ink drawings 
of birds, animals, and voyageurs add 
much pictorial appeal to these tales. 
Alfred A. Knopf, New York. 

Films 

AGES AND STAGES— 

a Canadian Film Board Production 

Last summer we needed a jumping 
off place lor a discussion on the char¬ 
acteristics of children, for our pre-camp 
training period. Somebody suggested 
‘Ages and Stages’, a Canadian Film 
Board production, and so wc investi¬ 
gated. The section heads had a pre¬ 
view and were very favourably 
impressed with the film which show 
age groups of normal children meeting 
the normal experiences in home, school 
and community. The section heads 
took notes and planned discussion. 
Even although the films were at least 
ten years old they were full of good 
situations, demonstrating age charac¬ 
teristics. 

During the training period, we 
showed all three films to the whole 
staff. They were given a briefing, tell¬ 
ing them what to look for, and to make 
notes. Afterwards they broke into small 
discussion groups divided on the basis 
of the ages with which they would be 
dealing. It worked exceedingly well. 

These films are easily procured from 
the film board outlets. It is just a 
matter of reserving them for a set date.

WHAT'S NEWS? 
Provincial Reports 

BRITISH COLUMBIA AND THE 
' CCA ANNUAL MEETING 
Their latest release catches us up 
. . . in the Presidents words: 

We have been working hard at the 
plans for the Canadian Camping- 
Association's Annual Meeting, and 
have planned this to take place in the 
context of a Seminar, as has been usual 
in the past. The information we have 
available at present is as follows: 
DATES: March 10th (evening) to 

March 13th (afternoon). 
1965. 

PLACE: Island Hall Hotel, Parks- 

villc, Vancouver Island. 
B.C. 

CONTENT: A central theme is diffi¬ 
cult to pin-point, but the 
Seminar will concentrate 
primarily on administra¬ 
tion and programming. 
Perhaps it would give 
you a picture if I tell you 
what the programme in¬ 
cludes:— 

A session on the over-all administration 
of a camp; discussion and open forums; 
sessions to do with Financing, Food 
Efficiency, Building and Maintenance; 
Legal Aspects; a pot-pourri of camp¬ 
ing skills, one evening only; a session 
of development of stafF relationships, 
growth of stafF, delegating of responsi¬ 
bilities. etc.; sessions in two sections for 
the “full-time paid staff person” and 
for the “part-time volunteer stafF per¬ 
son”; a session on Organizing and set¬ 
ting up of a programme; outtrips to 
Cathedral Grove and perhaps the bi¬ 
ological station; a session on evaluating 
your own camp programme: and a 
session where people in kindred groups 
can meet together — c.g. directors, 
nurses, waterfront people, programme 
directors, committee members, etc.; an 


62 


Canadian Camping 


address on “Leadership—the Keystone 
to Camping”. 

In each instance, we are being very 
firm about the fact that a key resource 
person be in each group, so that we 
will have content as well as informal 
sharing. This is vital, to our way of 
thinking. 

COST: $40.00 for accommoda¬ 

tion and meals in a 
beautiful seashore hotel. 
$10.00 for registration. 
Brochures arc in the process of being 
printed and we will see these are dis¬ 
tributed with all pertinent information 
re transportation, from Vancouver, etc. 
etc. 

MANITOBA NEWS 

From our next-door neighbour, 
speaking in Provinces, comes a list of 
the new Executive of the Manitoba 
Camping Association, plus an orchid 
for the Chairman of the Editorial 
Committee from MCA’s President, Mr. 
R. O. Douglas: 

“First, let me say how much we 
appreciate the tremendous amount 
of work someone must do in pub¬ 
lishing the C.C.A. Magazine. 
Many of the camps in Manitoba 
have benefitted and look forward 
to receiving the magazine.” 

CONFERENCE IN ONTARIO 

Plans for the Ontario Camping 
Association conference are nearly com¬ 
plete for their three-day meeting on 
February 25th, 26th and 27th at the 


Inn On The Park. A wide variety of 
topics appears on the proposed pro¬ 
gramme, highlighted by the Hon. 
William Davis, Minister of Education 
for Ontario. 

QUEBEC 

A recent letter from the Quebec 
Camping Association states that the 
membership has decided against a 
Camping Conference until the end of 
February, 1966.

Editors to the Rescue 

This issue of CANADIAN CAMP¬ 
ING comes to you on schedule (as 
did that of June 1964 also) because 
two former editors of the magazine. 
Mrs. G. W. Flynn and Miss Joyce 
Bertram, have stepped into the breach 
during two periods of illness sustained 
by your editor, Dorothy Douglas. We 
are fortunate indeed that, in any event, 
they have continued to give us the 
benefit of their experience by being 
active members of the Editorial Com¬ 
mittee. It is particularly gratifying 
that they were willing to take over on 
these two occasions when your editor 
went to hospital, and that they have 
offered to continue their assistance 
until she is able to resume her full 
responsibilities again. Mrs. Douglas ex¬ 
tends her warmest thanks to the Com¬ 
mittee in general, and particularly to 
these two members who arc giving her 
this invaluable help. 



E.F. J.B.

Cross Canada Centenary Journey 

from The Jesuit Relations , Carlton Library Series, McClelland & Stewart Ltd. Copyright 
1054 by Vanguard Press. Copyright \925 by Albert and Charles Boni , Inc. 


We hear it every year as each gaggle 
of canoes leaves the camp clock for 
parts unknown: “Don’t do this”, “Be 
sure to do that”, “Be careful of one 
thing,” “Pay attention to another”. So 
what else is new? Four hundred years 
ago they were saying the same things, 
perhaps from the very shores on which 
we stand, as the Jesuit Fathers travelled 
by canoe with the Savages of the day. 
Father Breboeuf, in his instructions to 
these intrepid gentlemen of the cloth, 
seemed to issue warnings not too differ¬ 
ent from those which concern trippers 
today . . . with one or two exceptions; 
like the food for instance: 

To conciliate the Savages, you must 
be careful never to make them wait for 
you in embarking. 

You must provide yourself with a 
tinder box or with a burning mirror, 
or with both, to furnish them fire in 
the daytime to light their pipes, and in 
the evening when they have to en¬ 
camp; these little services win their 
hearts. 

You should try to eat their sagamite 
or salmagundi in the way they prepare 
it, although it may be dirty, half- 
cooked and very tasteless. 

You must try and eat at daybreak 
unless you can take your meal with 
you in the canoe. 

You must be prompt in embarking 
and disembarking; and tuck up your 
gowns so that they will not get wet, 
and so that you will not carry cither 
water or sand into the canoe. To be 
properly dressed you must have your 
feet and legs bare; while crossing the 
rapids you can wear your shoes, and in 
the long portages, even your leggings. 

You must so conduct yourself as not 
to be at all troublesome to even one 
of these Barbarians. 

Each one will try, at the portages, 
to carry some litle thing, according to 


his strength; however little one carries, 
it greatly pleases the Savages, if it only 
be a kettle. 

Be careful not to annoy anyone in 
the canoe with your hat; it would be 
better to take your nightcap; there is 
no impropriety among the Savages. 

Do not undertake anything unless 
you desire to continue it; for example, 
do not begin to paddle unless you arc 
inclined to continue paddling. Take 
from the start the place in the canoe 
that you wish to keep. 

Finally understand that the Savages 
will retain same opinion of you in their 
own country that they will have 
formed on the, way; and one who 
passed for an irritable and troublesome 
person will have considerable difficulty 
afterwards in removing this opinion.

from page 63 

Campbell, President of the Nova Scotia 
Camping Association shows their en¬ 
thusiasm for the Centenary Journey: 

“The Centenary Journey is a sugges¬ 
ted plan by the Canadian Camping 
Association, as a means whereby 
campers might celebrate Canada’s 
Centennial Year, 1967. There are, 
in Canada today, a total of approxi¬ 
mately sixteen hundred camps in 
operation, annually serving approxi¬ 
mately 500,000 young Canadians. 
Some of these camps have been in 
operation since the late nineteenth 
century, and the Canadian Camping 
Association itself was incorporated 
in 1949. 

“There are three major aspects of this 
project: 1) to map and mark the 
transcontinental system of water 
routes which formed the famous 
Water Highways of exploration and 
commerce during the seveneenth and 
eighteen centuries; 2) to co-ordinate 
a programme of canoe trips during 
1967 along this entire transcontin¬ 
ental system. 3) to develop a pro¬ 
gramme of publicity which will make 
Canadians and visitors to Canada 
aware of these historic water routes, 
and encourage continued use of 
them in the years to come. In more 
general scope, it is hoped that such 
an appreciation of Canada’s unique 
heritage will foster and stimulate 
such concepts and goals as physical 
fitness, sportsmanship, wilderness 
conservation and recreation, all of 
which must play an increasingly im¬ 
portant and signficant part if Can¬ 
ada is to perform a truly effective 
role as it enters its second century 
as a respected member of the world 
community of nations.” 

Mrs. Campbell also submits the 
1964-5 Executive and Committee 
members:

66 


Canadian Camping 



from page 59 

Three years ago some young coun¬ 
sellors were chosen to help with morn¬ 
ing instruction because, as former 
campers, they had been interested in 
nature. During the pre-camp periods 
they are given a “refresher course”, 
but this time with a different approach. 
“How do we arouse and hold the in¬ 
terest of campers and make it fun?” 
There is often not the desired contin¬ 
uity in this counsellor group but we 
feel, even with the usual changes in 
staff, the plan is working well. The 
more we can catch and hold the in¬ 
terest of the senior campers, the more 
nature counsellors we will have in 
future years. Involving more coun¬ 
sellors in this way has made a more 
nature-oriented staff. During the sum¬ 
mer weeks spent together in the beauty 
of the camp setting, if staff and cam¬ 
pers share such interests, an awareness 
and appreciation of the marvellous 
plan of the Creator in the outdoor 
world will make the camp experience 
richer by far for everyone.
